Chapter 5: Spiritual Childhood—Trust, Surrender, and the Heart of the ‘Little Way’
As the years passed quietly in the convent, the idea of spiritual childhood stopped being just a metaphor. It became a real way of living. Imagine seeing yourself as a child before God—trusting completely, letting go of every fear and ambition, and simply resting in the knowledge that you’re loved, not for what you do, but just for being you.
Now, this isn’t about acting childish or ignoring reality. It’s actually a conscious choice—a decision to let go of self-reliance and bravely embrace dependence on a loving Father. Sometimes, though, that trust gets put to the test. Illness might return, bringing weakness and a heavy dose of uncertainty. The future? It’s blurry, and worries can feel overwhelming. But when those moments come, the practice of spiritual childhood offers a new way forward.
Instead of tightening your grip, trying to figure it all out or control every outcome, you choose to rest in the present. You accept each day as a pure gift. Slowly, the burdens of yesterday and the fears of tomorrow fade away. In their place, there’s this quiet confidence—almost like a whisper—that assures you everything will be alright.
This mindset changes everything—how you see yourself, and how you see others. You stop chasing perfection or craving recognition. Suddenly, you’re free to love without any fear holding you back. Those failures and shortcomings that used to feel so big? They lose their power. What really matters isn’t being successful, but staying faithful—just showing up, trying again, and trusting that even the smallest effort counts.
Picture this: after a long day filled with little frustrations, she sits quietly in the chapel, thinking about what it really means to be spiritually childlike. It hits her—being a child is about accepting your limitations, rejoicing in the Father’s love, and trusting that every need will be cared for. But here’s the thing: this kind of trust isn’t passive. It takes real courage to let go, to surrender control, and to believe—deep down—that love truly is enough.
That’s where the ‘Little Way’ shines brightest—in this steady attitude of trust and surrender. It’s a path that’s open to everyone, no matter your age or background. Most people assume holiness demands extraordinary effort, but what if the heart of the Christian life is actually a simple, loving relationship with God? To live as a child means resting in love, trusting in mercy, and believing that every moment—no matter how ordinary—can be transformed by grace.
